doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: The blues, swing and what counts as jazz
title: Playing the blues and its reach
summary: Rowe and Thomas talk about how fun and adaptable the blues is, its link to rock, and Muddy Waters's line.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: And you hear people moaning, yeah right. It’s so damn fun to play.
Absolutely. And folks who grew up with it knew it’s fun to listen to. You know you actually listen to it to get rid of the blues you know.
Yeah. One thing I love about playing the blues is you can’t get lost. I mean you really have to try to get lost.
You know you can feel it coming around again every time and —
It just lets you play without getting too distracted by trying to pay attention to complex chord changes and all that. Although you can make it complex also. So I think of it as
like the blues is like a chameleon. It’s like let’s play — we need something funky. Well we can play a 12-bar blues in funky. Or whatever. It can adapt.

Well absolutely. I mean that’s one of the things Ellington and so many others — you can play the blues all kind of which way. You can play it slow, you can play a stomp, fast blues, I mean all kind of different feeling and flavors and approaches is there with that fundamental blues. And then it connects — through like the pentatonic scale it connects to music around the world. So the blues is so fundamental to American music and like I say through the pentatonic scale it connects to music around the world. So then you have musicians who don’t want to confront the blues and you’re in America and you’re playing jazz? If you’re playing rock you can’t not confront the blues. If you’re playing country you can’t not confront the blues.
I remember Muddy Waters said, “The blues got pregnant and the baby was rock and roll.”

Yeah. Right, right, right, right. Yeah. Well then if the blues was — in that anecdote or metaphor if the blues was a woman then the father would be R&B. Because rock comes out of R&B. Especially through the person of Louis Jordan, who was jazz, R&B, entertainer, he had that whole thing.
